title: Trading the Fragmented World of 2026 - Systematic Investor - Ep.382

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Trading the Fragmented World of 2026 - Systematic Investor - Ep.382.docx

speakers: Rich Brennan (co-host, systematic trend follower, Australia)
summary: Two trend-following practitioners review 2025 (concentrated metals-led winners, April drawdown, short-term trend weak) and argue a fragmented, multipolar world suits trend following. Brennan then argues for trading the present with predefined rules (brakes and acceleration), treating forecasts as hypotheses, and avoiding tight optimisation.

coverage.note: intro, disclaimers, small talk, no content
fragmented spheres-of-influence world favours trend following; why imbalances persist
persistence over calm markets; resource fights; large Fed funds block trade (colour)
2025 review: concentration, metals attribution, laggards (FX, bonds, energy)
2025 lessons: diversification, familiar trend distribution, drawdown then recovery
true diversification incl. commodities, patience, 5y return and S&P correlation
short-term vs long-term lookback in 2025, ensemble models; agenda for the session
Formula 1 analogy: backtest average speed, brakes as commitments
brakes and acceleration; distinguishing rule exits from comfort exits
conservative sizing as always-on brake; future is unfinished not hidden
reflexivity, models cannibalise, precision as liability, emergence, trend following as participation

completeness_estimate: 0.88 - the first reader captured nearly every method and mechanism in the Brennan monologue (C08-C15) and the 2025 review; it missed small data points (false starts in Nifty, April drawdown recovery, monthly leader rotation, trend barometer) and the Stoic process-control point.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: conditions create trends. So markets don't move because someone predict predicts the future correctly. They move because something comes out of balance and stays that way long enough for prices to adjust.
claims.claim: Trends arise from imbalances that persist long enough for prices to adjust, not from correct forecasts.
claims.testable: partly - persistence of imbalances is testable via trend returns

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Central banks truncated trend moves before they could develop through coordinated intervention QE etc.
claims.claim: In the globalized era coordinated central bank action (QE) absorbed imbalances quickly and truncated trends, which made conditions harder for trend followers.
claims.testable: partly - needs a regime definition for coordination

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: energy shortages stay regional for longer. Um, inflation differs by country. Currencies reflect local stress, not global averages. Trade barriers persist. Sanctions last years, not weeks.
claims.claim: In a regionalized world release valves work slowly, so energy, inflation, currency and trade imbalances stay local and last longer, creating persistent trends.
claims.testable: partly - hard to define the regime ex ante

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: A regionalized world means more political shocks, sharper reversals, periods of chop when regional pressures offset each other.
claims.claim: A fragmented world raises the risk of political shocks, sharp reversals and choppy periods for trend followers, though the underlying structure still favours persistence.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I personally think Neils that we are in a period that suits our strategy probably better than anything we've seen in years.
claims.claim: Brennan judges the current fragmented-world period as the most favourable for trend following in years.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: which of the markets we will talk about this in a second that really made the difference in terms of performance. Uh it certainly wasn't the financial markets last year as such.
claims.claim: Fights over resources drive commodity trends, and in 2025 trend following performance came from commodity markets rather than financial markets.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there was a block trade in the January Fed funds futures of 200,000 contracts in one trade. That is by far the largest block trade ever recorded on the CME.
claims.claim: A record 200,000-contract single block in January Fed funds futures (previous largest about 84,000) signals a very large rates positioning; probably not a trend follower.
claims.indicator: CME Fed funds futures block size
claims.testable: no - single event, positioning not observable in public data

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: that attributed about 21% of total year's performance from metals alone and and gold was a standout not not through volatility or dramatic moves but through persistence.
claims.claim: In 2025 metals contributed about 21% of the benchmark trend portfolio's annual performance, led by gold via a persistent clean trend rather than volatility.
claims.testable: yes - sector attribution of a trend portfolio

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Our currencies dragged on our performance from policy divergence.
claims.claim: In 2025 currencies (policy divergence, Brazilian real reversal), bonds (rate uncertainty whipsaws) and energy (no persistent structure) lost money for the trend portfolio.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I regarded as a year of concentration so there were a small number of persistent trends that did the heavy lifting right throughout the year
claims.claim: In 2025 a few persistent trends produced most of the profit, i.e. returns were concentrated in a small number of markets.
claims.testable: yes - concentration of P&L across markets

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: with a diversified portfolio that's sitting there waiting like a trap. Um, whatever the opportunity is under that level of diversification, you will find that you're riding it
claims.claim: Since the location of the next outlier trend is unknowable, wide diversification ensures the portfolio is positioned to catch it and pay for losses elsewhere.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: to a large extent we had many relatively small losses but we have as you say concentration and a few big winners. That's classic trend following.
claims.claim: Trend following return distribution is many small losses and a few large winners, so a year like 2025 is typical.
claims.testable: yes - return distribution of trend index

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: at the end of June, the SG trend index touched its worst draw down ever in the 25 years of history.
claims.claim: The SG Trend Index hit (or nearly hit) its worst drawdown in 25 years at end of June 2025, then rebounded with six consecutive positive months in the speaker's program.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: wouldn't it be nice to have an a strategy in the portfolio that does not rely on prediction?
claims.claim: In an unpredictable world a non-predictive strategy such as trend following is a sensible portfolio component.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: If you were too concentrated in the liquid markets because you want to manage 1015 billion dollars, it would would have been much more difficult
claims.claim: Capacity-constrained large managers limited to the most liquid markets missed commodity trends, so a fully diversified smaller programme did better in 2025.
claims.indicator: assets under management vs market universe
claims.conditions: large AUM forced into liquid markets

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the first half was testing our patience as investors, right? So, we're rules based, but so we try to be super patient with our systems and then the second half it was all rewarded
claims.claim: Rules-based systems must be kept running through difficult stretches (Feb-Jun 2025) because payoffs came in the second half when opportunity arose.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we have delivered that average double-digit return with a correlation to the S&P of 0.15.
claims.claim: Trend following delivered double-digit average returns with about 0.15 correlation to the S&P 500 over 41 years, a diversifier to equity gains.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the concentration risk we have now in equity in indices like MSEI where it's like 70% US equities and then when you drill down it's like seven equities
claims.claim: Equity index concentration (about 70% US in the global index, dominated by about seven stocks) may push investors to diversify into trend following.
claims.conditions: equity bull market concentrated in few stocks

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was a pretty uh difficult year for short for the short-term traders index down about 5% or so uh last year.
claims.claim: Short-term trend followers lost about 5% in 2025 despite many surprises, contrary to the expectation that short horizons would benefit.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a short-term time frame say 20-day uh would have been hit the hardest last year. Having said that, had you had 60-day look back, you would have had a small positive.
claims.claim: In a same-universe simulation 20-day lookback lost most in 2025, 60-day was slightly positive, and 130-day and 260-day were negative, showing lookback choice matters year to year.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: that gives a a reason to perhaps consider ensemble models that that bring in the different time frames together because whilst you might not get the best performer, you you'll probably get a better average
claims.claim: Combining several lookback windows (ensemble) gives a better average outcome than picking one, and avoids luck in selecting the single best.
claims.testable: yes - compare ensemble vs single lookbacks

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Formula 1 race is not won by driving at the average speed of the track.
claims.claim: Trading to a historical average risk level is suboptimal; one should vary exposure with the conditions in front of you, like braking into corners and accelerating on straights.
claims.testable: partly - compare static vs conditional sizing

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: risk gets sized for historical calm. So sharp corners arrive too fast if they're not observed in the back test.
claims.claim: Sizing positions on backtest-average volatility leaves the portfolio exposed when volatility spikes beyond what the backtest contained.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: A trend that has further to run gets e exited because it has already exceeded what the back test suggested was normal.
claims.claim: Exiting winners because they exceed backtest norms cuts the long tail that trend following depends on.
claims.testable: yes - test exit cap on profits

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I'm not criticizing back testing as a tool because back testing is essential for understanding how systems behave. But the error is treating the back test as a map of the future
claims.claim: Backtests describe how a system behaved in the past and should not be used as a map of the future.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Brakes are not predictions. They're commitments. They exist before the corners appear.
claims.claim: Stop-losses, position limits and drawdown rules should be defined in advance and engage without debate, rather than being decided when losses occur.
claims.testable: yes - rules-based risk limits are testable

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: acceleration means staying on. It means allowing the straight to unfold without lifting your foot
claims.claim: Staying exposed while trend structure persists, even when profits look large, is what captures convexity.
claims.testable: yes - hold winners vs capped profits

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: can you articulate the rule that triggered the exit? If it's a rule you would have written before the trade, I believe that is risk management.
claims.claim: An exit is legitimate risk management only if it follows a rule written before the trade; exits invented after discomfort are rationalised emotion.
claims.testable: partly - audit of exits vs rules

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: So if you size so conservatively that no market condition can hurt you, you've also size so conservatively that no market condition can help you.
claims.claim: Permanently conservative sizing is an always-on brake that removes both downside and upside; variable braking (full exposure when structure supports it) is better.
claims.testable: yes - static vs variable sizing backtest

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: In the second view, which is the view I support, the future is not hidden. It is unfinished.
claims.claim: The future price path does not yet exist as it is built by participants' reactions, so better data cannot reveal it; the advantage is in responding.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: The market is reflexive. So if enough traders predict a price rise, they might buy and cause the rise.
claims.claim: Markets are reflexive: forecasts influence prices, so unlike physical systems prediction changes the outcome it targets.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: In markets, however, more traders using the same model make that model fail. Mean reversion systems, for example, cannibalize the signal over time as they are negative feedback processes.
claims.claim: As more traders use a mean reversion model it removes its own signal, because mean reversion is a negative feedback process.
claims.testable: partly - decay of signal over time

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the more assumptions you embed about conditions remaining similar. But when conditions shift and in an adaptive system they always shift, the precision therefore becomes a liability.
claims.claim: Tightly fitted models embed stationarity assumptions and become fragile when conditions shift.
claims.testable: yes - parameter sensitivity and out-of-sample tests

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: this is why trend following works. Not because we predict where markets will go, but because we participate in structures as they form.
claims.claim: Trend following works by recognising currently existing structure (persistence, volatility clustering) rather than forecasting.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I suggest that they think about forecasts as hypotheses rather than predictions.
claims.claim: Macro forecasts should be treated as hypotheses and traded only when the market confirms them (e.g. go short bonds only if bonds actually start to sell off).
claims.direction: trade in direction of confirming price move
claims.testable: yes - test macro signal with trend confirmation filter

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I'm saying the specific path or the exact sequence of prices, the magnitude of moves, the timing of reversals, that's not predetermined.
claims.claim: Statistical regularities (trend persistence, volatility clustering) exist, but the exact path, magnitude and timing are not predictable.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Every parameter has a justification. Every weakness appears addressed. The messiness of uncertainty is replaced by the satisfaction of completion
claims.claim: Optimisation gives an emotional feeling of completeness without removing real uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Stack enough assumptions together and you're no longer building a robust system. You're building a system that only works in a narrow band of conditions.
claims.claim: Accumulated calibration assumptions (moving-average length, vol target, patterns) make a system work only in the historical band and fail abruptly with hidden negative skew.
claims.conditions: conditions differ from the optimised period

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: convexity is not lost through error. It is surrendered to restore comfort.
claims.claim: Traders take profits early on working trends to relieve discomfort, giving up the convex payoff of trend following.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Good enough with robustness across conditions beats optimal almost every time.
claims.claim: Choose loosely optimised parameters from a plateau of similar results (e.g. 50 vs 200 day) rather than a precise historical optimum like 47 days.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the more you constrain your upside, the more you eliminate discomfort, the more you eliminate the asymmetry that makes trend following profitable.
claims.claim: Smoothing the equity curve by optimisation or sizing reduces the positive asymmetry that makes trend following profitable; costs are deferred and statistical.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: if the system you trade requires you to make calm, rational decisions under pressure, your system has a design flaw
claims.claim: Systems should be designed so discretionary emotional decisions are not needed.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: predetermined entries and exits, automated execution where possible, position sizing that keeps losses tolerable regardless of emotional state.
claims.claim: Remove emotional pressure points via predetermined entries/exits, automation and size that keeps losses tolerable; treat strong emotions as a signal to redesign the system (e.g. reduce size).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: India's nifty50 was actually one of the worst performers in our portfolio but we had these repeated false starts that never developed
claims.claim: Markets that produce repeated false starts (breakouts that never develop into sustained trends) are where a trend portfolio loses money even when the wider equity complex is modestly positive, as with India's Nifty 50 in 2025.
claims.direction: trend followers lose in whipsaw (false-start) markets
claims.conditions: fails when signals trigger repeatedly without follow-through; equity P&L in 2025 was modest but positive with Japan the leader and the US mixed
claims.testable: yes - count of failed breakouts per market versus trade P&L

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: That was our worst draw down historically we've had um for our particular approach. But from that period on fortunately we had the the metals that recovered us.
claims.claim: An event shock (the April 2025 Liberation Day tariff announcement) produced the largest historical drawdown for an outlier-hunting trend programme, and the recovery came from a persistent trend in one sector (metals), which is why broad sector diversification is needed to recoup shock losses.
claims.conditions: recovery requires at least one sector with a persistent trend after the shock
claims.testable: yes - drawdown and recovery attribution by sector around the April 2025 event

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the consistency and the rotation of where these opportunities came from. One month it was being short JGBs, one month it was being long gold
claims.claim: In the H2-2025 rebound the profits rotated across markets month by month (short JGBs, then long gold, then long silver), so trend profits depended on holding a wide book that could pick up each new leader rather than on a single theme.
claims.direction: short JGBs, long gold, long silver in successive months
claims.conditions: works when leadership rotates across asset classes
claims.testable: yes - monthly P&L attribution by market

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there was a lot of writing back then um you know once again calling for the death of trend following and all of that stuff
claims.claim: Calls for the death of trend following clustered at the June 2025 drawdown trough, just before six straight positive months, so obituaries tend to arrive at the worst moment and abandoning a rules-based programme at a drawdown extreme would have missed the recovery.
claims.conditions: applies to allocators deciding whether to cut a trend programme after a record drawdown
claims.testable: partly - forward returns of CTA indices after record drawdowns; few independent episodes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: yesterday my trend barometer finished at 52. That's a strong start so far.
claims.claim: The host's Trend Barometer (a proprietary gauge of how well trend followers are doing) read 52 on 2026-01-06 while the SG CTA and Trend indices were up about 1.5% and the short-term traders index gained less because of its lower volatility; the barometer is used as a quick read on industry conditions.
claims.indicator: Trend Barometer; SG CTA Index; SG Trend Index; SG Short-Term Traders Index
claims.testable: partly - barometer construction is not given in the transcript

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: having diversification in terms of models and not just time frame and markets and all of that stuff. I I really do.
claims.claim: Diversification should be applied across model types as well as across lookback time frames and markets, because no single lookback or model is reliably best year to year.
claims.testable: yes - compare multi-model blends with single models across years

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: your entry rules they are up to you. Your exit rules are up to you. Your position sizing is up to you. Your decision to follow your process is up to you.
claims.claim: Trend followers should control only what is controllable (entry rules, exit rules, sizing, adherence to the process) and release attachment to outcomes such as whether a given trade wins or the trend continues, which removes anxiety and the urge to override.
claims.testable: no - a psychological framing rather than a measurable relationship
